VMH damage causes hyperphagia and obesity in the absence of any change in feeding patterns and that this obesity is not prevented by intragastric pair-feeding procedures that eliminate the oropharyngeally evoked cephalic phase of digestion.

the mechanisms that produce the metabolic abnormalities that follow VMH lesions.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
VMH obesity and hyperinsulinemia are independent of feeding pattern and that they result from a metabolic bias that may be independent of the cephalic phase of digestion.
VMH lesions cause obesity and hyperinsulinemia in rats regardless of the pattern of food delivery.
VMH lesions induce obesity, hyperinsulinemia, and a metabolic bias favoring lipid accumulation in the absence of disturbances in either food or water intake or in the temporal patterns of feeding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
VMH obesity and hyperinsulinemia are caused by an intrinsic metabolic bias, and that the cephalic phase responses of digestion do not play a role in the pathogenesis.
the VMH is a critical site of metabolic bias favoring fat accumulation, but the bias is not dependent upon oropharyngeally induced cephalic responses to food.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the VMH lesion is an effective way to produce obesity and hyperinsulinemia in the rat.
the VMH obesity syndrome is a metabolic disorder of fundamental origin, and it is not a consequence of the hyperphagia or other behavioral sequelae that accompany VMH damage.
the cephalic phase of digestion is not a critical factor for the development of the metabolic syndrome that follows VMH damage.
